title: F-Stop Magazine submissions
eligibility: Photographers worldwide; image and issue rules vary.
compensation: Publication; the official guidelines state there is no payment for included images.

source_text: Submission Guidelines for F-Stop Magazine - A fine art photography magazine featuring contemporary photography from established and emerging photographers Visit F-Stop's Facebook page Visit F-Stop's Instagram page Visit F-Stop's Shop Email F-Stop submission guidelines ISSUE #140: Portfolio 2026 December/January Issue #140 will be a Portfolio issue. A portfolio should be a single project or body of work. DEADLINE: November 10, 2026 Submit 12-20 photographs along with a project statement following the guidelines below. Issue #140 will have an expected publication date of December 1, 2026. Only one submission per person for an issue. ISSUE #141: Abstraction 2027 February/March Issue #141 will explore abstraction in photography. DEADLINE: January 8, 2027 Submit up to 12 photographs following the guidelines below. Issue #141 will have an expected publication date of February 1, 2027. Only one submission per person for an issue. * If the current theme/s do not fit your work check back for future issues. PLEASE READ AND FOLLOW CAREFULLY THE GUIDELINES BELOW (scroll down) Please be careful not to resubmit images that have already been published in f-stop Please do not write your information or file names in all CAPITAL LETTERS Please limit your submission to 12 images, no more ( unless that issue's guidelines ask for more) Note: It is free to submit photographs to an issue of F-Stop. There is no payment for images that are included in an issue. 1. Image File Specifications: jpg files only 1200 pixels for the LONGEST edge For a horizontal picture = width For a vertical picture = height File size around 500kbs or smaller, please optimize your images for web This is done easily using Photoshop Export > Save for Web See below for detailed instructions or how to optimize for web with various software No borders or watermarks - Please do not include borders or watermarks, ask if you have questions about what is acceptable Instructions for saving your images for web in various software applications - here . 2. File Naming: Please name the files with your first name and last name (given name then surname) and a number. Use the same name that you list in your email as your name. No spaces, dashes, parenthesis or other non letter/number characters. You can put an underscore or dash between first and last name if you would like. Please check that you did not put an extra .jpg in your file name, if your computer hides file extensions try checking the file name after you attach it to your email.     name.jpg NOT name.jpg.jpg Example for "Susan Smith" = SusanSmith1.jpg,  SusanSmith2.jpg etc. 3. Email: Subject line of your email should indicate which issue you are submitting your work to - issue # and issue name Please send your images in 1 email Please try to attach the image files not embed them, a zip file can be used if your application only embeds files. Embedded files do not always show up in the email when it loads, some files may be missed as a result. A zip file is fine, no .rar files please Please do not share them using Google Drive, or other file sharing applications Please put all submission information  as text in your email not as attached documents. Only images should be attached. Please do not send PDFs or other text files. 4. Please Include With Your Entry: Name - not in all capital letters please. First (given) name, then Last (surname) name. Location - where you live currently Titles for your photographs in a numbered list. Please write out EACH title as you would want it to appear. If they all have the same title write out each one. Please have the list numbers match your file numbers. You can include a series or project name with each title. Keep in mind titles can be a great way to provide context for your work if it is part of the group exhibition. URL for your portfolio website if you have one. We dont include social media, blogs or non portfolio sites at this time. Please spell out the full URL Contact information - If you do not have a portfolio site URL you can provide an email address OR instagram handle  This will be used on the contributors page if your work is included. If the issue you are submitting to has the theme "Portfolio" you will also need to include a project statement for your work. For other issues it is optional. Submissions Email: [email protected] If you have any questions or have difficulty sending your images please email for help. COPYRIGHT INFORMATION: By submitting photos for publication in F-Stop Magazine you are stipulating to us that you own copyright to these photographs or have permission from the copyright holder to submit these photographs. You are granting F-Stop Magazine a non-exclusive license to use the photograph in its submitted form, subject to re-sizing to fit the magazine format, for publication on the F-Stop website for as long as the website exists. Please note that back issues of F-Stop may remain available in the archive for as long as the website exists. If an image is used as a cover to the magazine you are granting F-Stop Magazine permission to use it for promotion on sites such as  facebook.com and to put the f-stop logo on it. None of the photographs may be downloaded, stored, printed, manipulated, distributed, or used in any form without prior written permission from the copyright holder. Works published on this website are protected under domestic and international copyright laws and are not considered to be public domain. Take-downÂ (unpublish) requests As a matter of editorial policy, we do not unpublish content from past issues. Please do not submit photographs you do not want published online. See Copyright information above. F-Stop's past issues continue to be online indefinitely. OPTIMIZING IMAGES FOR THE WEB: The goal of optimizing your image files for the web is to have images  that load quickly and look great. For our purposes, your image files should be 1200px for the longest edge and then saved as a compressed JPG with the resulting filesize typically around 400 or 500kb (an image with a lot of fine detail may be larger). To do this in Photoshop Go to Image > Image Size and you will get a pop up box. In this box first make sure “Resample Image” at the bottom of the box is checked. Then set the longest edge in “Pixel Dimensions” to 1200 pixels. After you have sized your image you next want to optimize the file  size. In current versions of Photoshop you can do this using "Export" File > Export > Export As In the dialog that opens choose Format: JPG Quality: 70 Image Size: set the longest edge to 1200px if you have not already done this. Color Space: Convert to sRGB Click Export In older versions of Photoshop you can do this with the “Save for Web” option. File > Export > Save for Web (or in older versions it is File > Save for Web & Devices) In the dialogue box that opens you want to make sure JPEG is chosen for  the file type Then set the Quality to 70 . Optimized, Embed Color Profile and Convert to sRGB should already be checked. Click Save and it will ask you where to save this optimized version of your file. Optimizing in other image softwareâ¦. Lightroom Go to File > Export Under File Settings choose Image Format JPEG, Color Space sRGB, Quality 70 Under Image Sizing check Resize to Fit Choose “Long Edge” Check Don’t Enlarge. Put in 1200 pixels for the first box then next to Resolution put in 72 pixels per inch Click Export Preview (mac) Open the file in Preview Go to Tools > Adjust Size Change the dimensions measurement to pixels (the default is inches) Make the longest edge  1200 pixels. Next you want to save it as a JPG with the quality low enough to make  the file size around 800k or smaller but not so low that the image looks bad -Â you may have to experiment. Go to File > Save as Choose where to save the image then where it says Format choose JPEG Set the Quality slider to the 7th or 8th | mark and save To verifiy the file size go to the Finder and Command + I to see the file info. Gimp Gimp is an open source image editing application Go to Image > Scale Image Set  the longest edge 1200 pixels Click Scale Go to File > Export Choose where you want to save it and what to call it Click Export In the Export Image as JPEG popup choose Quality 70 Click Export Other options ImageOptim open source image optimization app that you can use to compress files that have been sized to the 1200px for the long edge dimension or to further compress a file. Go to the settings under the "Quality" tab and check "Enable lossy minification" Move the JPG Quality slider to about 3/4 of the way to the right Then, just drag the file to the app and it will optimizes it saving it in the same place Squoosh.app in browser image otpimization app that allows you to size the file dimensions and compress using quality 70. A note for using this: if you resize the dimensions in the app the preview of the file will appear distorted, but if you download the optimized file and view it you will see it is not distorted. ▲

source_text: Introducing the 2026 CatchLight Global Fellowship jury | CatchLight Skip to content Subscribe Donate General News Introducing the 2026 CatchLight Global Fellowship jury Date February 13, 2026 Share Share on X (Opens in new window) X Share on Facebook (Opens in new window) Facebook Share using Native tools Copy link Copied to clipboard Each year, the CatchLight Global Fellowship awards three visual storytellers with grants of $30,000 and access to development and networking opportunities. Now in its ninth year, CatchLight continues to search for creative leaders who are committed to visual storytelling as a tool for long-term impact. This year’s application attracted a record-breaking 509 submissions from candidates from 34 countries. To help guide our selection process, we have invited leaders from across the visual media landscape to participate in our fellowship jury. The 2026 CatchLight Global Fellowship jury Johanna Alarcón Photojournalist and 2024 CatchLight Global Fellow Website: johannaalarcon.com |     Follow: @johis.alarcon About Johanna Alarcón + Johanna Alarcón is a photojournalist and visual storyteller based in Ecuador whose work is focused on social justice, human rights, identity, and gender-related issues. In addition to the 2024 CatchLight Global Fellowship, she has received awards and honors from World Press Photo, National Geographic, Magnum Foundation, among other prominent institutions in the field of photography. Her work has been featured in The New York Times, Smithsonian Magazine, National Geographic, The Wall Street Journal, The Guardian, and many other publications, and her work has been exhibited worldwide. text goes here Lisa Kleiner Chanoff Co-founder Catapult Film Fund Website: catapultfilmfund.org |     Follow: @catapultfilmfund About Lisa Kleiner Chanoff + Lisa Kleiner Chanoff is co-founder and president of Catapult Film Fund, an organization that supports nonfiction filmmakers with early-stage funding and mentorship. Before filmmaking, she practiced law in San Francisco and with the Civil Rights Division of the U.S. Department of Justice in Washington, D.C. Lisa also has a master’s degree in museum studies. Her executive producer credits include documentaries Watchers of the Sky, Art and Craft, Brimstone and Glory, When God Sleeps, Extremis, Life Overtakes Me, and Lift, as well as narrative features Burn Country, Fruitvale Station, Loves & Taxes, The Outside Story, and Western. She also serves on the boards of SFFILM, CatchLight, and The Redford Center, and is an advisor to the Close Up Initiative for filmmakers from Southwest Asia and North Africa. Lisa is a member of the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences. Abby Chen Contemporary Curator at Asian Art Museum Website: asianart.org |     Follow: @asianartmuseum About Abby Chen + Abby Chen is an internationally recognized curator, educator, writer and community organizer, and the Asian Art Museum’s first head of contemporary art. Chen was previously the artistic director at the Chinese Culture Center of San Francisco, where she helped transform the organization through risk-taking exhibitions, process-driven practices, and impactful public art. She was the curator for the Taiwan Pavilion at the 2024 Venice Biennale. She is the recipient of the 2024 National Art Education Association Asian Art and Culture Interest Group Distinguished Art Educator Award. Her experimental approach often explores the intersectionalities of race, sexuality, gender, nation, migration, and technology in the United States and Asia. She holds an M.A. in visual and critical Studies from the California College of Arts. Ala Kheir Photographer, curator and educator Website: alakheir.com |     Follow: @ala.kheir About Ala Kheir + Ala Kheir is a photographer and educator whose work actively engages with his home country, Sudan. Through his photography, he creates personal perspectives and narratives that reflect his immediate surroundings. He has been actively engaged with the Sudanese photography archives, researching, archiving, restoring, and exhibiting the work of photographers like Elsharif Aboud and Abbas Habiballah. He also has been involved in training and networking for photographers in Africa, notably with the Centers of Learning for Photography in Africa in Johannesburg, South Africa. Kheir is a co-founder of the Sudanese Photographers Group. Currently, he runs The Other Vision (TOV), a photography platform that focuses on photography education, training, and amplification of young Sudanese photographers. Through TOV, he engages with the public in an attempt to address social issues and change in Sudan. Sophie Parker Director of Photo London Website: photolondon.org Follow: @__sophie.parker__ @photolondonfair About Sophie Parker + Sophie Parker is the director of Photo London, which she joined in 2018 as the Gallery Development Manager and later became associate director before assuming her current role. Prior to Photo London, Parker worked at Alan Cristea gallery, RA Magazine, and Lewisham Local History Society. She has curated and organized exhibitions, events and workshops, ranging in a variety of subjects from fine art, photography and performance art to history and politics. She has a Masters degree in Anthropology and Cultural Politics from Goldsmiths, University of London and a BA Honours in History of Art and Design from Manchester Metropolitan University. source_text: CatchLight invites visual storytellers worldwide to apply for 2026 Global Fellowship | CatchLight Skip to content Subscribe Donate General News CatchLight invites visual storytellers worldwide to apply for 2026 Global Fellowship Date November 5, 2025 Share Share on X (Opens in new window) X Share on Facebook (Opens in new window) Facebook Share using Native tools Copy link Copied to clipboard Three visual practitioners to receive $30,000 awards and opportunities to strengthen their impact. From the project, “Of the Fields.” © Adam Perez / CatchLight Global CatchLight will open submissions for the 2026 CatchLight Global Fellowship , beginning November 15 through December 15, 2025. Each year, the Fellowship awards $30,000 grants to three innovative visual storytellers whose work is a tool for information, connection and transformation in their communities. Application opens on Nov. 15 The Fellowship supports innovative visual storytellers who seek to cultivate meaningful audience engagement and amplify the impact of their work through inventive distribution strategies. Acting as an incubator, the program provides financial support, fosters professional development, and builds networks that empower creative leaders to influence the future of visual storytelling. The 2026 Fellows will be selected by an international jury and announced at the CatchLight Visual Storytelling Summit in May 2026. Applications are free and open to all nationalities. More information at catchlight.io/global . From the project, “From the Ashes, I Rose.” © Rehab Eldalil / CatchLight Global “In a moment when division so often dominates the headlines, CatchLight stands firm in our belief in the unifying power of images. Through the CatchLight Global Fellowship, we are supporting visual storytellers around the world who are deeply connected to their communities — photographers who are building bridges across lines of experience, geography, and perspective. Their work fosters dialogue, empathy, and a renewed sense of shared humanity,” said Elodie Mailliet Storm, CEO of CatchLight. The 2025 CatchLight Global Fellows continue to redefine documentary storytelling by centering community voices. Cairo-based Rehab Eldalil has been engaging SWANA war survivors through photography and mixed media to highlight resilience and global solidarity. Uruguayan Federico Estol collaborates with La Paz shoeshiner communities, now training participants as storytellers to amplify visibility and break stigmas. Central California-based Adam/n Perez partners with farmworker communities to document labor, land, and climate challenges, sharing their stories through photography, video, and public installations. Since May 2025, each has expanded their work, gaining new platforms and community-driven initiatives that extend the impact of their original projects. From the project, “Heroes del Brillo.” © Federico Estol / CatchLight Global “As an independent photographer and filmmaker working alongside migrant farmworkers during a time of mass deportation, the CatchLight community has been an anchor in the chaos,” said Adam/n Perez. “Their support has gone far beyond professional guidance — it has been a source of care, understanding, and solidarity. Through their mentorship, I’ve discovered new ways to gather stories with greater tenderness and thoughtfulness. CatchLight has given me the space to sit with the grief and trauma that surround this work, and to transform that pain into stories that honor the resilience of my community.” For Federico Estol, “CatchLight is the only platform in photography that lets me expand my practice through long-term community projects with freedom, guidance, and new ways of connecting with people as visual storytellers, always in a non-extractive way. Their support has been precious, because so few platforms allow for sustained projects that combine education with street-level action to address social challenges like marginalization, discrimination, and polarization. CatchLight prioritizes people and civic engagement over marketing or commercial success.” TIMELINE November 15, 2025: Applications open December 15, 2025: Applications close May 2026: Announcement of the Global Fellows at the CatchLight Visual Storytelling Summit in San Francisco UPCOMING EVENTS Night of Photojournalism in Austin Saturday, November 15, 2025 7:30 – 9:30pm CST 800 Congress Ave. Austin, TX 78701 Get Tickets The Night of Photojournalism in Austin, presented as part of the Texas Tribune Festival , will feature conversations with leading journalists—including award-winning photographers John Moore, Adriana Loureiro Fernández, Ilana Panich-Linsman, and reporter Perla Trevizo. Large-scale projections of photo essays by local and international journalists will be accompanied by live music by Gary Jules and Kyle King. Night of Photojournalism in Paris Saturday, November 15, 2025 7:30 – 8:30pm CET Gaîté Lyrique, 3bis Rue Papin 75003 Paris, France Get Tickets Presented in partnership with Dysturb as part of Reporters Without Borders’ 40th anniversary celebrations, the Night of Photojournalism in Paris will feature a 360° immersive experience combining large-scale projections, live DJ sets, and conversations with leading voices in visual journalism. Through powerful imagery and sound, the evening explores urgent global issues through the lenses of photojournalists from around the world. source_text: Magnum Foundation Grantees Shortlisted for Paris Photo–Aperture PhotoBook Awards — Magnum Foundation Expanding creativity and diversity in visual storytelling Magnum Foundation Grantees Shortlisted for Paris Photo–Aperture PhotoBook Awards Photo by Daniel Salemi / Aperture Congratulations to Magnum Foundation grantees and friends Newsha Tavakolian , Miranda Barnes , Bieke Depoorter , and Sohrab Hura , for making the Paris Photo-Aperture 2026 PhotoBook Awards shortlist ! The shortlisted books will be exhibited at Paris Photo, open to the public from November 11 through November 15, followed by an international tour, including in Dublin at PhotoIreland, December 2026, and other venues to be announced. See more about the books below. Photo by Daniel Salemi / Aperture Miranda Barnes Social Season Important Flowers, London Design by Anamaria Morris Shortlisted for “First PhotoBook” category. Miranda Barnes’s debut book explores the rich history of Black cotillions in the US through an immersive collection of photographs made at debutante balls in Detroit between 2022 and 2025. This poignant and elegant body of work documents the community, camaraderie, and anticipation of this custom and the moment of transition it hinges upon. Photo by Daniel Salemi / Aperture Bieke Depoorter The Beds I Slept In Hannibal Books, Antwerp, Belgium Design by Armand Mevis and Bieke Depoorter Shortlisted for “PhotoBook of the Year." In this intimate book, Bieke Depoorter looks back on years of overnight stays with complete strangers. Each bed symbolizes a fragile balance between trust, safety and the unknown. Photo by Daniel Salemi / Aperture Newsha Tavakolian And They Laughed at Me Kehrer Verlag, Heidelberg, Germany Design by Kehrer Design, Laura Pecoroni Shortlisted for “PhotoBook of the Year." For And They Laughed at Me, Newsha Tavakolian trawled through her archives not to pick her best work, but instead to dig up what she refers to as her “eyesore” photos from the early days of her career, when, at the age of sixteen, she had started to work as a photojournalist in Tehran. Revisiting these “eyesore” images against the backdrop of again terrible events, what emerges is a clear rite of passage from the hope and dreams of youth, towards the disappointment of reality and the conclusion that there is only one real choice in life. To be drawn to darkness, or to choose to fight the darkness and go towards the light. Photo by Daniel Salemi / Aperture Sohrab Hura Snow MACK, London Design by Sohrab Hura Shortlisted for “PhotoBook of the Year." Sohrab Hura’s Snow documents his repeated visits to the Indian-administered region of Kashmir over a five-year period, recording its passage through the three distinct phases of its winter. Across photographs of Kashmir’s landscapes and communities, picturesque imagery often gives way to residual markers of conflict and violence. title: Announcing the 2026 Counter Histories: Puerto Rico Fellows
eligibility: Varies by programme; some calls are regional.
source_text: Announcing the 2026 Counter Histories: Puerto Rico Fellows — Magnum Foundation Expanding creativity and diversity in visual storytelling Announcing the 2026 Counter Histories: Puerto Rico Fellows Rubén Rolando Para español, desplácese hacia abajo. Magnum Foundation is proud to announce the eight fellows selected to participate in the 2026 cycle of Counter Histories: Puerto Rico, our new multiyear initiative supporting photographic projects that engage with archives and collective memory of Puerto Rico and its diaspora. They are: Alexis Gines Andina Marie Osorio Ángela Sophia Milá Erika P. Rodríguez George Malave Juan Carlos Rodríguez Rubén Rolando Tamara Cedré At a time when public memory in Puerto Rico is under threat due to systemic disinvestment and cultural erasure, artists have taken a leading role in resisting this silencing. This initiative seeks to strengthen the role photography can play in building a collective visual archive that centers the perspectives of those on and with ties to the archipelago. Clockwise from top left: Alexis Gines, Andina Marie Osorio, Ángela Sophia Milá, Erika P. Rodríguez, George Malave, Juan Carlos Rodríguez, Rubén Rolando, and Tamara Cedré The selected fellows were chosen from 216 applications, via an open call and nomination process. The final cohort was chosen by a selection committee that included members of the Magnum Foundation team as well as Aldeide Delgado, founder and director of Women Photographers International Archive (WOPHA); Abdiel Segarra, artist, researcher, and Curator at Museo de Arte Contemporáneo de Puerto Rico; and Susanna Temkin, Senior Curator at El Museo del Barrio. This year’s fellowship cohort is the first chapter of a three year initiative, which will include a symposium in San Juan with the Museo de Arte Contemporaneo de Puerto Rico , as well as additional future grantmaking and public programming in Puerto Rico, New York City, and beyond. “I am incredibly thrilled and grateful for the opportunity to form part of the first Counter Histories: Puerto Rico cohort,” notes Ángela Sophia Milá. “At such a crucial moment for Puerto Rican stories and for the preservation of history, it is more important than ever to celebrate and honor the legacies of place and personhood that continue to shape Boricua identity. I am incredibly excited to work with a cohort of artists who are committed to challenging traditional histories and producing art that is intrinsically tied to their sense of place and identity. I look forward to growing as an artist throughout the coming months and for the opportunity to carry out a project that I have been envisioning for years now.” As selection committee member Abdiel Segarra shared, “the selected projects focus on the everyday lives of communities and individuals who have historically been represented from the top down, rather than through their own voices and experiences. In that sense, the perspectives brought together through this initiative open a window into the heart of the archipelago, the inner life of diasporic neighborhoods, and the intimate emotional networks that give meaning to daily life—beyond the official pages of history books and the headlines of newspapers. In present-day Puerto Rico, cultural institutions continue to face a profound crisis shaped by systemic neglect, government disinvestment, and the erosion of public resources. Preserving the memories of people who have long understood the importance of their own stories is therefore more than an act of documentation. It is a way of creating the conditions for a fuller understanding of our past, while renewing the points of reference from which we interpret its echoes in the present.” As we welcome this remarkable cohort, we are deeply saddened to share that one of the selected fellows, Juan Carlos Rodríguez, passed away shortly after beginning this fellowship. Rodríguez was a beloved member of the Puerto Rican documentary film community and an ardent archivist of Viequense history. He was passionate about studying documentary traditions in Latin America, particularly how they represented the social issues of their time. His proposed Counter Histories project Terrestrial Futures: Possible Returns to the Vieques Civil Disobedience Camps brings together his 1999 photographs of the occupation of US Navy bombing ranges in Vieques, offering a way to understand “the complex realities of the Puerto Rican archipelago in the present.” His work is particularly timely as the archipelago is being remilitarized to serve as a launching pad for the US interventions in the Caribbean and Venezuela. To learn more about Rodríguez and his archive of work, see here and here . Read more about the selected fellows and their projects below: Ángela Sophia Milá Utuado: entre el monte y el olvido Building a community archive to centralize and celebrate the forgotten histories of the town of Utuado for community access now and in the future, including through an exhibition of the photographic archive of the artist’s late grandfather, Ismael Pérez Colón. “How can locals be empowered to celebrate their archives? How can we challenge narratives of Puerto Rican rurality through the elevation of forgotten family photos? How can we begin the process of centralizing these archives for the community’s use now and in the future?” Rubén Rolando After Forgetting Activating photographs made by Rolando’s stepmother during the 1980s and 1990s in Puerto Rico to explore how vernacular photography can preserve women’s histories, queer childhoods, and everyday life as historical evidence within the island’s colonial context. “More than preserving photographs, I seek to honor our permanence in the archipelago, our relationship to territory and habitat, and our capacity to document our own lives as historical evidence. In Puerto Rico, the personal is political, and family photographs remind us that everyday life is also part of our collective history.” George Malave Family Relations Digitizing and sharing over five decades of Malave’s photographic works on Puerto Rican life and culture in the diaspora. “How can we recognize and learn from those who arrived from a different place and culture, without reducing them to ‘the other?’ How do we learn to see one another as if in a mirror, with equal dignity and worth?” Erika P. Rodríguez Fotopleneros: Ricardo Alcaraz Díaz Working with photojournalist Ricardo Alcaraz Díaz's 50-year archive, this project reconstructs the oral memory, history, and music embedded in his images of la plena — a working-class musical tradition whose living practitioners remain largely outside the official record. “What stories emerge when you return a photograph to the people in it, and open a space to build a record by those who lived it? The counter-history here is not a correction of the record, it is that the record was never made.” Alexis Gines Through The Grapevine “My father was killed in an East Harlem drug war in the early 1990s when I was 11 months old. Using three generations of family archive as both research and visuals, I am making work acknowledging the presence of absence, which hopes to reimagine what life might have looked like if my father survived.” Andina Marie Osorio Untitled Activating recovered VHS tapes left behind by the artist's late Tia Esther Ramos in her Co-Op City apartment. Migrating from Puerto Rico to the Bronx in her late teens, Ramos recorded cable networks from the 1980s to early 2000s, ranging from public broadcasts to The Macy’s Day Parade, Walter Mercado’s infamous astrology readings, a documentary on El Gran Combo legendary song “Brujería,” to the three-part E News broadcast of the Selena Murder trial. “My interest lies in the incidental memories and ancestral energies evoked by her ephemera in the feminine domestic setting, along with the contribution these lost narratives make to the greater diasporic Puerto Rican culture and archive." Tamara Cedré No Puedo Ver El Fondo | I Can't See The Bottom Constructing a counter-archive that reveals how colonialism, tourism, and resource management have shaped Puerto Rico's relationship to water. “By engaging both the representational and material histories of the medium, I investigate how photography has shaped not only ways of seeing the landscape, but also the ecological conditions it seeks to depict.” Juan Carlos Rodríguez Futuros terrenales: Retornos posibles a los campamentos de desobediencia civil de Vieques Drawing attention to the 1999 civil disobedience camps protesting US Navy bombing rangings in Vieques. Rodríguez’s archive of images, made during his time participating in the camps, invites reflection on the possible futures of these territories. “In this project, my goal is to give more visibility to the history of Vieques as a military target range, while expanding the discussion about how military training at home ends up reproducing violence and dissolving the border between the state of war and peace. It hopes to change distorting views about colonialism, land tenure, and other issues while making visible the links among war, environmental harm, military toxicity, health disparities, and cancer.” ABOUT THE INITIATIVE Since 2018, Magnum Foundation’s Counter Histories initiative has supported artists who elevate suppressed histories, reframe dominant narratives, and challenge the power structures embedded in archives. By exploring the creative possibilities offered by the gaps, absences, and silences in historical records, Counter Histories offers an expanded and collaborative approach to historical inquiry and photographic storytelling—and suggests the radical possibilities of alternative narratives. Building on this longstanding initiative, Magnum Foundation is thrilled to be partnering with past Counter Histories fellow Christopher Gregory-Rivera on this new edition of the program focused on Puerto Rico and its diaspora. The initiative is co-led through a partnership between Magnum Foundation and the newly launched Instituto de Observación Colectiva , an organization founded by Gregory-Rivera that aims to support visual practitioners in Puerto Rico and its diaspora. Alongside Gregory-Rivera, this initiative has been developed with the input of an esteemed advisory of photographers, curators, and historians with expertise in histories and visual cultures of Puerto Rico, the Caribbean, and their diasporas, including: Abdiel Segarra, Aldeide Delgado, Ali Rosa-Salas, Deepak Lamba-Nieves, Iberia Pérez González, Jorell Meléndez-Badillo, and Laura Bravo López. We are also grateful to our ongoing working group of photographers and past grantees who shared their input on the open call and structure of the program. Read more about the process here . As we launch Counter Histories: Puerto Rico, we are deeply grateful to the Mellon Foundation for their generous support of this initiative, and to the Museo de Arte Contemporaneo de Puerto Rico , who will host the closing symposium for the program. Magnum Foundation’s initial Counter Histories fellowships were developed with the generous support of the Henry Luce Foundation . Anunciado el Grupo de Artistas de Contrahistorias: Puerto Rico 2026 La Fundación Magnum se enorgullece en anunciar les ocho artistas seleccionades para participar en la edición del 2026 de Contrahistorias: Puerto Rico, nuestra iniciativa plurianual apoyando proyectos fotográficos que abordan el archivo y la memoria colectiva de Puerto Rico y su diáspora. Elles son: Alexis Gines Andina Marie Osorio Ángela Sophia Milá Erika P. Rodríguez George Malave Juan Carlos Rodríguez Rubén Rolando Tamara Cedré En un momento donde la memoria pública en Puerto Rico se ve amenazada por la desinversión sistemática y el borrado cultural, artistas han liderado la resistencia a este silenciamiento. Esta iniciativa busca fortalecer el rol que la fotografía juega en construir un archivo visual colectivo que se centra en la perspectiva de aquelles viviendo en y con lazos al Archipiélago. En sentido del reloj: Alexis Gines, Andina Marie Osorio, Ángela Sophia Milá, Erika P. Rodríguez, George Malave, Juan Carlos Rodríguez, Rubén Rolando, and Tamara Cedré Les artistas seleccionades fueron escogides de 216 solicitudes a través de un proceso de convocatoria pública y nominación. El grupo final fue decidido por un comité que incluyó miembros del equipo de la Fundación Magnum y Aldeide Delgado, fundadora y directora del Archivo Internacional de Mujeres Fotógrafas (WOPHA); Abdiel Segarra, artista, investigador y curador en el Museo de Arte Contemporáneo de Puerto Rico; y Susanna Temkin, Curadora Principal en el Museo del Barrio. El grupo de este año marca el primer capítulo de esta iniciativa de tres años, que incluirá un simposio en San Juan con el Museo de Arte Contemporáneo de Puerto Rico , al igual que futuras subvenciones y programación pública en Puerto Rico, Nueva York y más lugares. «Estoy increíblemente emocionada y agradecida por la oportunidad de formar parte del primer grupo de Contrahistorias: Puerto Rico», dice Ángela Sophia Milá. «En este momento tan crucial para historias Puertorriqueñas y la preservación de la historia, es más importante que nunca celebrar y honrar los legados del lugar y condiciones que continúan forjando la identidad boricua. Estoy muy entusiasmada por trabajar junto a un grupo de artistas que están comprometidos con cuestionar la historia tradicional y producir arte que está intrínsecamente atado a su sentido de pertenencia y persona. Tengo ansias de verme crecer como artista a lo largo de los próximos meses y por la oportunidad de llevar a cabo un proyecto que llevo visionando por años.» Como miembro del comité de selección, Abdiel Segarra comparte: «los proyectos seleccionados se enfocan en las vidas de las comunidades e individuos que no han sido históricamente representados a través de su propia voz y experiencia. En ese sentido, las perspectivas reunidas en esta iniciativa abren una ventana al corazón del Archipiélago, la vida íntima de los barrios diaspóricos, y las redes afectivas que dan sentido a la vida cotidiana — más allá de las narrativas oficiales de los libros de historia y los titulares de periódicos. En el Puerto Rico actual las instituciones culturales se enfrentan a una crisis profunda creada por el descuido sistemático, la desinversión gubernamental y la erosión de recursos públicos. Preservar las memorias de personas que siempre han entendido la importancia de sus propios relatos es entonces más que una documentación. Es una manera de crear las condiciones para entender más de lleno nuestro pasado mientras renovamos los puntos de referencia de los cuales interpretamos sus ecos en el presente.» Mientras damos la bienvenida a este maravilloso grupo estamos profundamente tristes en compartir que uno de los artistas, Juan Carlos Rodríguez, falleció poco después de comenzar el programa. Rodríguez fue un miembro querido de la comunidad de cine documental y un archivista incansable de la historia viequense. Tenía pasión por estudiar tradiciones del cine documental en Latinoamérica, en particular cómo representan temas sociales de sus épocas. El proyecto que propuso para Contrahistorias: Puerto Rico, Futuros terrenales: Retornos posibles a los campamentos de desobediencia civil de Vieques, reúne sus fotografías tomadas en 1999 de la ocupación de los campos de bombardeo de la marina estadounidense para ofrecer una manera de entender «la realidad compleja del archipiélago puertorriqueño en el presente.» Su trabajo es particularmente relevante dado que el archipiélago está siendo remilitarizado para servir como base para las intervenciones estadounidenses en el Caribe y Venezuela. Para aprender más sobre Juan Carlos y su archivo visita este enlace y este . Lea más sobre los artistas seleccionades y sus proyectos a continuación: Ángela Sophia Milá Utuado: entre el monte y el olvido Construir un archivo comunitario para centralizar y celebrar la historia olvidada del pueblo de Utuado con acceso para la comunidad ahora y en el futuro, e incluye una exhibición del archivo fotográfico del abuelo de la artista, Ismael Pérez Colón. «¿Cómo pueden los locales ser empoderados para celebrar sus archivos? ¿Cómo podemos cuestionar narrativas sobre la ruralidad puertorriqueña a través del enaltecimiento de fotos familiares olvidadas? ¿Cómo podemos comenzar a centralizar estos archivos para el uso de la comunidad ahora y en el futuro?» Rubén Rolando Después del olvido Activando fotografías tomadas por la madrastra de Rolando durante los 1980s y 1990s en Puerto Rico para explorar cómo la fotografía vernácula puede preservar historias de mujeres, las niñeces queer y la cotidianidad como evidencia histórica dentro del contexto colonial de la isla. «Más que preservar una fotografía, busco honrar nuestra permanencia en el archipiélago, nuestra relación con el territorio y hábitat, y nuestra capacidad para documentar nuestras propias vidas como evidencia histórica. En Puerto Rico lo personal es político, y las fotos familiares nos recuerdan que todos los días son también parte de nuestra historia colectiva.» George Malave Relaciones familiares Digitalizar y compartir más de cinco décadas del trabajo fotográfico de Malave sobre la vida y cultura puertorriqueña en la diáspora. «¿Cómo podemos reconocer y aprender de esos que han llegado de una cultura y un lugar distinto sin reducirlos a un “otro”? ¿Cómo aprendemos a vernos uno al otro como en un espejo, con igualdad de dignidad y valor?» Erika P. Rodríguez Fotopleneros: Ricardo Alcaraz Díaz Trabajando con el archivo del fotoperiodista Ricardo Alcaraz Díaz que abarca cincuenta años de trabajo, este proyecto rescata la memoria e historia oral, al igual que la música contenida en sus imágenes de la plena– una tradición musical obrera cuyos practicantes vivos a menudo permanecen fuera de la historia oficial. «¿Qué historias emergen cuando regresas una fotografía a las personas que captura y abres espacio a la construcción de una historia por quienes lo vivieron? La contra historia en este caso no es una corrección del archivo sino que el archivo nunca se creó.» Alexis Gines A través de la vid «Mi padre fue asesinado en una guerra de drogas a principios de los 1990s cuando yo tenía once meses. Usando tres generaciones de archivos familiares como investigación y visuales, estoy creando para reconocer la presencia de la ausencia, con la esperanza de reimaginar cómo se hubiera visto mi vida si mi padre hubiera sobrevivido.» Andina Marie Osorio Sin título Activando pietaje de VHS que dejó la tía difunta de la artista, Tía Esther Ramos, en su apartamento de Co-Op City. Migrando al Bronx de Puerto Rico en su adolescencia, Ramos grabó los canales televisivos de cable desde los 1980s hasta principio de los 2000s, variando de transmisiones públicas hasta la Parada de Macy’s, las lecturas famosas de Walter Mercado, un documental sobre la canción legendaria de El Gran Combo «Brujería», hasta la transmisión de tres partes de la cadena E News sobre el juicio del asesinato de Selena. «Mi interés está en las memorias incidentales y energías ancestrales que rescata la efémera de ella en el contexto doméstico femenino, y cómo estas narrativas pérdidas llegan más ampliamente a la cultura y archivo diaspórica.» Tamara Cedré No Puedo Ver El Fondo Construyendo un contra archivo que revela cómo el colonialismo, el turismo y el manejo de recursos han afectado la relación de Puerto Rico con el agua. «Usando la historia material y de representación del medio, investigo cómo la fotografía ha informado no solo las maneras de ver el paisaje sino también las condiciones ecológicas que busca representar.» Juan Carlos Rodríguez Futuros terrenales: Retornos posibles a los campamentos de desobediencia civil de Vieques Llamando la atención a los campamentos de desobediencia civil en contra de los campos de bombardeo de la marina estadounidense del 1999 en Vieques. El archivo de imágenes de Rodríguez, capturadas durante su tiempo participando de los campamentos, invita a reflexionar sobre los futuros posibles de estos territorios. «Con este proyecto mi meta es darle más visibilidad a la historia de Vieques como un campo de bombardeo y tiro, y a su vez expandir la discusión sobre cómo el entrenamiento militar reproduce la violencia y disuelve la línea entre el estado de guerra y la paz. El proyecto busca cambiar las actitudes distorsionadas sobre el colonialismo, tenencia territorial, y otros temas mientras hace visible los lazos entre la guerra, daño ambiental, toxicidad militar, desigualdades de salud, y el cáncer.» SOBRE LA INICIATIVA Desde 2018, la iniciativa de Counter Histories de la Fundación Magnum ha apoyado artistas quienes elevan historias suprimidas, reencuadran narrativas dominantes y cuestionan las estructuras de poder que se encuentran en los archivos. Explorando las posibilidades creativas que ofrecen las lagunas, ausencias y silencios en los archivos históricos, Counter Histories ofrece una metodología expandida y colaborativa para la investigación y narrativas fotográficas– y sugiere las posibilidades radicales de narrativas alternas. Construyendo sobre los cimientos de esta iniciativa la Fundación Magnum se enorgullece en asociarse con Christopher Gregory-Rivera, artista seleccionado en una edición previa de Counter Histories , en construir esta nueva edición del programa enfocada en Puerto Rico y su diáspora. La iniciativa es co-dirigida a través de una asociación entre la Fundación Magnum y el recién creado Instituto de Observación Colectiva, una organización creada por Gregory-Rivera que busca apoyar la creación visual en Puerto Rico y en su diáspora. Junto a Gregory-Rivera, esta iniciativa ha sido desarrollada con el insumo de un comité de estimados asesores incluyendo fotógrafes, curadores, e historiadores con conocimiento en las historias y cultura visual de Puerto Rico, el Caribe, y sus diásporas. Incluye: Abdiel Segarra, Aldeide Delgado, Ali Rosa-Salas, Deepak Lamba-Nieves. Iberia Pérez González, Jorell Meléndez-Badillo, y Laura Bravo López. También estamos agradecidos a nuestro grupo de trabajo de fotógrafes y subvencionades que nos ayudan a mejorar el formato de las convocatorias y la estructura del programa. Lea más sobre el proceso aquí . Lanzando Contrahistorias: Puerto Rico, estamos sumamente agradecidos a la Fundación Mellon por su apoyo generoso de esta iniciativa, y al Museo de Arte Contemporáneo de Puerto Rico , que acoge el simposio de cierre del programa. Los ciclos iniciales de Counter Histories de la Fundación Magnum fueron desarrollados con el apoyo generoso de la Fundación Henry Luce . source_text: Announcing the 2026 Inge Morath Award — Magnum Foundation Expanding creativity and diversity in visual storytelling Announcing the 2026 Inge Morath Award Dara Petrova Magnum Foundation, Magnum Photos , and the Inge Morath Estate are pleased to announce Dara Petrova as the recipient of this year’s Inge Morath Award. Petrova will receive a $7,500 production grant to support the completion of her project, Circle. This year’s finalist, Alice Poyzer, will receive a $1,000 grant in support of her project Other Joys. Born in 1997, Izmail, Ukraine, Dara Petrova is a documentary photographer. Petrova obtained a Master’s degree in Law from Odesa Law Academy in 2020, specializing in Social Security Law. She started photographing after fleeing Ukraine, and is interested in how individuals invent new forms of solidarity for themselves, exhaust themselves, fall into depression, or love one another. Dara Petrova Petrova’s project, Circle , captures the gaze of a local woman on everyday life in Ukraine during the war years, who, “like all the others, feels guilty for being alive, guilty for not contributing enough, guilty for not winning, guilty for being a woman and escaping conscription so easily.” Documenting Kyiv techno raves held between curfews, veteran rehabilitation, soldier tattoos, and funeral ceremonies, Circle channels the internal state of those living here. “The pain is no longer only in the physical or material damage of the war, it is in what we inflict on ourselves to show that we are still alive.” This project was selected from a pool of over 100 applications by the members of Magnum Photos. Given each year to a woman or nonbinary photographer under the age of 30, the award honors the legacy of their colleague, Inge Morath . Dara Petrova Dara Petrova On receiving the award, Petrova shared, “My initial reaction was shock, which gradually gave way to a warm sense of joy in my chest. This programme will allow me to devote myself much more calmly and freely to my photography without having to juggle it with my day job.” This year’s finalist, Alice Poyzer, is being recognized for her long-term project Other Joys, which describes the joy behind her special interests and the difficulties she faces as an autistic woman. Poyzer is a British photographer making post-documentary, constructed, and portrait images, working with both analogue and digital methods. Since graduating in 2025 with a Master's in Photography from the University of the West of England, Poyzer has gone on to win the British Journal of Photography's Female in Focus Award. Her images recently shown at Paris Photo under the Carte Blanche Award and WePresent's Spring Show at London's Copeland Gallery. Alice Poyzer Alice Poyzer Alice Poyzer On being named a finalist, Poyzer shared: “I am honoured to receive recognition from Magnum… The grant will make it possible to attend shoots across the UK that I previously have not been able to afford travel and access to.” Congratulations to these two outstanding photographers. To follow more of their work, visit their websites at darapetrova.com and alicepoyzer.com . Guest User August 6, 2026 Facebook 0 Twitter LinkedIn 0 Reddit Tumblr Pinterest 0 0 Likes

source_text: One World, One Game: Communities Celebrate the World Cup in NYC — Magnum Foundation Expanding creativity and diversity in visual storytelling One World, One Game: Communities Celebrate the World Cup in NYC Sara Konradi This summer, Magnum Foundation partnered with Storyline for One World, One Game , a storytelling project unfolding across New York City throughout the 2026 World Cup. We gave grants to five local photographers who documented how communities experience the tournament and how New York becomes a gathering place for the world. See images from the five projects below! Walaa Yassien: A Thread of Belonging “Living in New York as a Sudanese refugee, I realized I was looking for places that felt familiar [...] Sudan has never played in a FIFA World Cup. This year, as the national team came closer than ever to qualifying while the country endured a devastating war, it is hard not to imagine what that moment would feel like. Seeing Senegal, Morocco, Egypt, Algeria, Cape Verde, and other African and Arab nations represented carried a different kind of meaning for me. I wasn't only watching as a photographer. I was celebrating alongside communities that, in different ways, also carry home with them wherever they go.” An Ecuadorian mother holds her child among supporters gathered at Boulevard Junction in Jackson Heights, Queens, during the Mexico vs. Ecuador match, June 30, 2026. Families, children, and supporters of different generations gather together in Astoria, Queens, to watch Egypt compete in the 2026 FIFA World Cup, June 26, 2026. The gathering transforms a neighborhood space into a shared place of celebration and connection. A Senegalese supporter stands beside a handwritten note referencing “Lions de la Teranga,” the nickname of the Senegal national team, during the Senegal vs. Iraq match gathering in Harlem, New York City, June 26, 2026. A Senegalese supporter holds the national flag after Senegal’s victory over Iraq during a World Cup gathering in Harlem, New York City, June 26, 2026. A young Mexican supporter celebrates after Mexico’s victory over Ecuador at Boulevard Junction in Jackson Heights, Queens, June 30, 2026. A handwritten note beside him reads: “It’s a personal and unique experience that I will remember in these final moments. Signed, Víctor.” A football café in Bushwick, Brooklyn, fills with supporters watching Morocco face the Netherlands during the 2026 FIFA World Cup, June 29, 2026. A Mexican supporter stands among the crowd at Boulevard Junction in Jackson Heights, Queens, holding a handwritten note that reads “I am happy to be Mexican” during the Mexico vs. Ecuador match, June 30, 2026. A portrait of Aron, the son of Edward Scissorkicks player William, during a match with the Ecuadorian football league team at Brooklyn Bridge Park, New York City, June 27, 2026. Destiny Mata: United by the Block “As a second-generation Mexican American artist raised in the Lower East Side of Manhattan, photographing World Cup gatherings became deeply personal. I was raised in public housing, where many residents are surrounded by fenced-off green spaces that remain inaccessible, limiting opportunities to connect with our neighbors. That experience has shaped both my life and my work, and it has fueled my commitment to advocating for public spaces that truly belong to the people who live there. While documenting the World Cup watch parties, I found myself drawn to the ways fútbol fans took up space and activated streets and sidewalks [...] The World Cup created energetic spaces where culture, identity, and community become visible, bringing to life city streets where people can gather, celebrate, and remember what it feels like to experience euphoric joy and loss together.” A skateboarder cruises through the streets of Bushwick, Brooklyn, proudly waving a Mexican flag after Mexico’s victory over Czechia during the 2026 FIFA World Cup outside Football Café on June 24, 2026. Mexico vs Ecuador fútbol watch party takes over the streets of Bushwick, Brooklyn, outside Football Café, hosted by Migo Events and POC Fútbol Brooklyn, 2026 FIFA World Cup in Bushwick, Brooklyn, July 3, 2026. Taco truck workers celebrate Mexico's victory over Ecuador during the 2026 FIFA World Cup watch party hosted by Migo Events and POC Fútbol Brooklyn in Bushwick, Brooklyn, July 3, 2026. A street vendor grills tacos al pastor while World Cup fans watch the Mexico vs Czechia match outside the Jefferson Street L train station in Bushwick, Brooklyn, on June 24, 2026. A young Ecuadorian fútbol fan watches alongside cheering fans during Ecuador's 2026 FIFA World Cup match against Germany beneath the elevated Junction Boulevard 7 train on Roosevelt Avenue in Jackson Heights, Queens, June 25, 2026. Fans watch the Mexico vs. Ecuador match on an iPad screen propped on a makeshift cardboard box atop a car during the 2026 FIFA World Cup in Bushwick, Brooklyn, July 3, 2026. A couple dances in celebration of Mexico’s victory over Czechia during the 2026 FIFA World Cup in the streets of Bushwick, Brooklyn, on June 24, 2026. Fútbol fans take over the streets to watch a 2026 FIFA World Cup match at an outdoor watch party, where the game is broadcast on screens mounted to a converted ambulance beneath the elevated Junction Boulevard 7 train on Roosevelt Avenue in Jackson Heights, Queens, June 25, 2026. Fan blows a horn and proudly waves the Mexican flag during the Mexico vs. England match on the sidewalk in Sunset Park, Brooklyn, July 5 2026. Richard Louissaint: The Joy and Resilience Continues “In the midst of an administration bent on making Haitians' lives harder here and in their home country, the solidarity and representation of Haiti during the World Cup was hard to miss. From the [styles] that were created specifically for the games and the ways the Haitian flag was worn, pride and resilience was everywhere.” Fans watched Morocco vs Haiti 4-2 in FIFA World Cup Group C. In Haiti's last game of the Cup at Haiti Cultural Exchange. Haiti made their first goals in the tournament. June 24, 2026. Fans at the Haiti vs. Brazil viewing party at Herbert Von King Park in Brooklyn which Haiti lost, ending their run. June 19, 2026. Fans at the Haiti vs. Brazil viewing party at Herbert Von King Park in Brooklyn which Haiti lost, ending their run. June 19, 2026. Haiti Cultural Exchange in Brooklyn redesigned their space for the World Cup for viewing parties and to promote the designs of two Haitian designers, Garvenchy Nicolas and Maison Demar. Fans at the Haiti vs. Brazil viewing party at Herbert Von King Park in Brooklyn which Haiti lost, ending their run. June 19, 2026. Fans at the Haiti vs. Brazil viewing party at Herbert Von King Park in Brooklyn which Haiti lost, ending their run. June 19, 2026. Kisha Bari: Morabeza- Cabo Verde in Brooklyn “Group H of the 2026 FIFA World Cup included Spain, Uruguay, Saudi Arabia and a tiny island nation off the West Coast of Africa, Cabo Verde. Who or where is Cabo Verde?! People were asking. With a population of just over half a million people, they put together a team and qualified for their first ever FIFA World Cup [...] [In Bedford-Stuyvesant, Brooklyn,] September Cafe subsequently became a huge hub for the Cape Verdean World Cup games [...] Cape Verdeans came from as far away as Connecticut, Massachusetts and Vancouver, and [the owner, Sara Lopes] had to purchase two extra TVs to set up outside the cafe.” Lelo Roche sings the Cabo Verde National Anthem ahead of their first game against Spain. Bed-Stuy, Brooklyn, June 15, 2026. Despite neither team scoring a goal, Cabo Verdeans see this as a major win against football giants, Spain, in a 0-0 result. Bed-Stuy Brooklyn, June 15, 2026. Ana Samedo during a tense moment in the game. Bed-Stuy, Brooklyn, June 15, 2026. Maria Miranda's cachupa. A Cabo Verdean stew that includes beans, yuka, pork, hominy and greens. To most Cabo Verdeans, cachupa is the taste of home.  Bed-Stuy, Brooklyn, June 26, 2026. Sarah Lopes celebrates with Nova Moon and Miles. Bed-Stuy, Brooklyn, June 15, 2026. Sara Lopes and Ana Samedo join the celebratory dance party in the cafe. Sara is wearing tchabeta (waist cloths) which are a Cape Verdean cultural tradition worn during the batuku dance.  Bed-Stuy, Brooklyn, June 15, 2026. As the watch party has grown in significant numbers since the first game, Sara has had to prepare her cafe hours ahead of kick off time. Bed-Stuy Brooklyn, June 26, 2026. The crowd grew to around 300 people after halftime and everyone feels the tension. Bed-Stuy, Brooklyn, June 26, 2026. Lelo Roche glued to a tense moment in the game between Cape Verde and Saudi Arabia. Bed-Stuy, Brooklyn, June 26, 2026. The kids in the crowd hit the pavement with chalk to express their heritage and support. Bed-Stuy, Brooklyn, June 26, 2026. Sara Konradi: Far from Watan, Close to Home “This project documents moments of community connected to parts of the SWANA diaspora in New York during the 2026 FIFA World Cup. The word وطن  (Arabic pronunciation: waṭan, Persian pronunciation: vatan) means homeland, native land, country, or place of origin. Far from Watan, Close to Home explores the contrast between the physical distance from the homeland and the emotional closeness experienced through gatherings, television screens, and shared sounds across the city – whether it’s a street in Astoria, a bar in Bay Ridge, a soccer field in Brooklyn Bridge Park, or an apartment in Ditmas Park.” Tonya, Fabrice, Emily, Elif, Siham, Elizandan, Ariane and Michael react to the Morocco-Haiti match at a home watch party in East Flatbush, Brooklyn, on June 24, 2026. source_text: Open Call: Fall 2026 New York City Fellowship — Magnum Foundation Expanding creativity and diversity in visual storytelling Open Call: Fall 2026 New York City Fellowship Manmeet Kaur (11) and Ammy Kaur (11) posing for a portrait after participating in a turban tying competition at a gurdwara in New Jersey on May 10th, 2026. Photo by Roshni Khatri. We're accepting applications for the Fall 2026 session of the New York City Fellowship, a program offering a project production grant, mentorship, and arts administration experience to NYC-based early-career photographers and photojournalists. Recognizing the challenges of making a living as a working photographer, this fellowship serves a unique dual purpose: supporting the development of the fellows’ photographic projects, while also providing them with paid work experience in Magnum Foundation’s office. This fellowship is designed for early-career photographers looking for an opportunity to deepen, expand, and complete an NYC-based project that speaks to social issues. During the fellowship, fellows produce an in-depth photography project with mentorship from the Magnum Foundation team. Fellows are encouraged to build relationships with the communities they are photographing, build partnerships with relevant organizations, and experiment with narrative forms and storytelling techniques. Fellows receive mentorship and project development support from Magnum Foundation staff and our extended network throughout the duration of the fellowship. Fellows meet with the MF team bi-weekly to share progress and get feedback on their documentary photography project. In addition to producing a project, fellows gain arts administration by spending two days a week working in the Magnum Foundation office. Fellows are considered an integral part of Magnum Foundation’s team and are expected to make significant contributions to the day-to-day work we do at Magnum Foundation, and to use this time to learn more about the running of an arts nonprofit. The fellows work on a range of projects in the New York office including research on social issues, exploration of emerging technologies and platforms, multimedia production, and event production. Candidates should have expertise in at least one of the following areas: arts administration, research, writing, video production, or graphic design. Candidates will be paired with Magnum Foundation projects according to their expertise and interests. In addition, fellows’ responsibilities include working and photographing periodic evening events. Proposed projects should be based in New York City, speak to social issues, and engage with NYC-based communities. We encourage applications from people who have at least one completed long-term project, including recent graduates and self-taught photographers. This program is open to photographers of all ages. Eligibility Duration The fellowship runs for 12 weeks from mid-September to mid-December. Exact start dates and finish dates will be agreed upon with the selected fellow. Fellows will be expected to produce and complete a documentary photography project in NYC during the fellowship. Fellows are required to spend Wednesdays and Thursdays (16 hours per week) working with the MF team in Magnum Foundation’s NYC office. There may be occasional requirements to attend evening events at the MF office. COMPENSATION $5,000 production grant provided at the beginning of the fellowship to cover costs associated with the production, completion and distribution of your NYC-based project. An additional $25/hr for the 16 hrs/week spent in-office on arts administration work, paid bi-weekly . The fellowship is designed for New York City based photographers and does not provide room and board or transportation. Apply Applications are due September 1, 2026 at 11:59 PM ET. Fellows are chosen by an internal selection committee. You will need to submit your resume, a cover letter, a project proposal, and an edit of past work. Any questions can be addressed to submissions@magnumfoundation.org . A decade ago, she chose to listen to her inner child and pursue her dream of becoming a photographer, leaving behind a prolific career in architecture—a field that shaped her understanding of visual language and urban space. Inspired by Georges Perec’s concept of the infraordinary, her work critically examines everyday life, uncovering the complex layers hidden beneath overlooked stories. She is the founder of Observadores Urbanos, a platform dedicated to promoting Latin American street and documentary photography while building a community of visual storytellers in the region. Through this initiative, she edited Antología de Fotografía de Calle Mexicana, the first book of its kind in Mexico. Her work, which spans various photographic approaches, has been published in The Guardian, La Vanguardia, Gatopardo, and L’Oeil de la Photographie, among others. In addition to collaborating with Reuters and various agencies, media outlets, and NGOs, she has exhibited in over fifty shows across four continents and has received awards in prestigious national and international photography competitions. Sandra is a member of Women Photograph, The Raw Society, and Women Street Photographers, and she is an alum of the Eddie Adams Workshop. She is also the official photographer of La Carrera Panamericana and a Fujifilm ambassador—a role that allows her to inspire and support fellow photographers while continuing to evolve in her own practice. Alongside her photographic work, she is a faculty member at Tecnológico de Monterrey, leads photography workshops in various countries, and speaks at international photography festivals. Learn more about her by visiting her website: vitaflumen.com Queretaro, Mexico 6 Photos Diego Fabro Diego Fabro is a Brazilian fine art photographer based in Dublin, Ireland. All of his personal photographic work revolves around the theme of "Home," exploring the nuances of spatial, temporal, and psychological perception between life in Brazil and Ireland. In the recent years, his work has been showcased in prominent exhibitions at the Photo Museum Ireland, PhotoIreland Festival, and the Royal Hibernian Academy in Dublin. Publications featuring his work include TIME Magazine, The British Journal of Photography, and European Photography Art Magazine. His artistic contributions have been recognized through acquisitions for permanent art collections, including The National Photography Collection (PhotoMuseum Ireland) and the State Art Collection (OPW) in Ireland. Dublin, Ireland 6 Photos Tatiana Lopez Tatiana is an Ecuadorean photographer, multidisciplinary artist, and visual anthropologist. Her work focuses on the role places, and memory play in the construction and deconstruction of identity, women’s issues, the body as a medium of expression, and the interconnectedness between humans and nature. Following her background in visual anthropology, she is interested in incorporating ethnographic methods in visual storytelling. Her research interests include, indigenous peoples animistic practices, body-territory relations in connection to indigeneity, and the study of human/non-human relations through dreams. At the core of her practice she hopes to incorporate collaborative methods of storytelling and creatively use photography and filmmaking as powerful tools to raise awareness about environmental issues, equality and women’s rights. For Tatiana photography is her journey of self-discovery, connection, meditation, understanding and transformation.
